title: classify signaling type (juxtacrine/paracrine/autocrine/endocrine) from experimental results
stem: Researchers study how cell type X signals to target cells T in culture. (1) When X cells are mixed with T cells and touch them, T cells turn on gene Y. (2) When medium in which X cells grew for 24 hours is added to a separate dish of T cells, gene Y stays off. (3) When X and T cells share a dish but are separated by a porous membrane that lets proteins pass but prevents cell contact, gene Y stays off. (4) When T cells are treated with an antibody that blocks their receptor, touching X cells no longer turns on gene Y. Which best classifies the signaling from X to T?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contact-dependent (juxtacrine) signaling, because a signal on the surface of X binds the receptor on T only when the cells touch.
choices.rationale: Correct: the response needs direct contact (results 1 to 3), and a receptor on T is required (result 4), so a membrane-bound signal on X binds a receptor on T.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paracrine signaling, because X releases a diffusible signal that acts on nearby T cells.
choices.rationale: A diffusible signal would have crossed the porous membrane and would have worked in the conditioned medium, and neither of those turned on gene Y.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endocrine signaling, because X releases a signal that travels through the fluid to distant T cells.
choices.rationale: A signal carried in fluid would also have worked in the conditioned medium and across the porous membrane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autocrine signaling, because X cells respond to a signal they make themselves.
choices.rationale: Autocrine signals act on the cell that makes them, but here it is the T cells that respond and only when touched.

title: classify signaling type (juxtacrine/paracrine/autocrine/endocrine) from experimental results (variant 1)
stem: In a developing tissue, a small group of cells secretes protein P. Cells within about 100 µm of the group turn on gene G, including cells that do not touch the group. Cells farther than 200 µm away do not respond. Protein P is broken down by enzymes in the extracellular fluid within minutes. When the group of cells is transplanted to a new site, cells within 100 µm of the graft turn on gene G. Which best classifies this signaling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endocrine signaling, because a secreted protein travels to target cells in other parts of the body.
choices.rationale: Endocrine signals are carried by the bloodstream to distant tissues, and here P is degraded locally and acts over 100 µm only.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paracrine signaling, because a short-lived secreted signal acts only on nearby cells.
choices.rationale: Correct: nearby cells respond without touching, the response falls to zero with distance, and P is degraded quickly, which describes a local diffusible signal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contact-dependent signaling, because the responding cells must be in direct membrane contact with the group.
choices.rationale: Cells that do not touch the group still respond, so direct contact is not required.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autocrine signaling, because the cells that secrete P are the ones that respond to it.
choices.rationale: The responding cells are neighbors of the signaling group, so the signal acts on other cells and not just on the cells that make it.

title: classify signaling type (juxtacrine/paracrine/autocrine/endocrine) from experimental results (variant 2)
stem: A tumor cell line makes growth factor G and has receptors for it. Single cells plated one per well, far from any other cell, still divide in medium with no added growth factor. Adding an antibody that binds and neutralizes G to the medium stops their division, and so does an antibody that blocks the G receptor. Which best classifies the signaling that drives division in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Paracrine signaling, because G acts on nearby cells.
choices.rationale: Paracrine signaling needs a different nearby cell to receive the signal, and each well has only one cell.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autocrine signaling, because the cell makes a signal that binds its own receptors.
choices.rationale: Correct: each well holds only one cell, so the signal can only come from the cell itself and act on the same cell's receptor; blocking either G or its receptor stops division.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contact-dependent signaling, because G is attached to the membrane of the neighboring cell.
choices.rationale: There is no neighboring cell to touch, since each cell is alone in its well.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endocrine signaling, because G is carried through fluid to target cells.
choices.rationale: Endocrine signaling involves a distant target cell reached by the bloodstream, and no such cell exists in a culture well.

title: classify signaling type (juxtacrine/paracrine/autocrine/endocrine) from experimental results (variant 3)
stem: A gland is removed from a rat, and the rat's liver cells stop breaking down glycogen. When a piece of the gland is transplanted under the skin of the ear, 20 cm from the liver, glycogen breakdown resumes. Skin cells next to the graft, which lack the receptor for the gland's hormone, show no response. Which statement best explains these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hormone acts as an autocrine signal, so only the gland cells in the graft respond to it.
choices.rationale: The response is seen in liver cells far from the graft, so the signal acts on cells other than the ones that make it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hormone acts as a paracrine signal, so the response depends on how close the target cells are to the graft.
choices.rationale: The liver is 20 cm from the graft and still responds, and nearby skin cells do not, so distance from the source does not decide the response.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hormone acts as an endocrine signal: it travels in the blood to distant cells, and only cells with the receptor respond.
choices.rationale: Correct: the graft is far from the liver yet restores the response, so the signal travels through the blood; neighboring skin cells without the receptor do not respond, so the receptor determines which cells respond.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hormone acts through direct cell-to-cell contact, so the graft must have grown into the liver.
choices.rationale: The graft is under the skin of the ear and responds across 20 cm, so contact between the graft and liver cells is not possible.

title: separate ligand binding from cell response using a results table
stem:
Ligand L binds a single receptor protein, R, which an antibody test shows is present on the surface of cell types 1, 2 and 4. Cell type 3 does not make R. A researcher adds L at the same concentration to each type.
Cell type | Labeled L bound | Response to L
1 | high | breaks down glycogen
2 | high | opens an ion channel
3 | none | none
4 | high | none
Which conclusion is best supported by all four rows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The structure of L alone determines the response, so L should cause the same response in every cell that binds it.
choices.rationale: Cell types 1 and 2 bind the same ligand yet respond differently, so the ligand's structure does not fix the response.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding to R is necessary but not sufficient: the response depends on the transduction proteins and effectors each cell type has, so the same ligand and receptor can give different responses or none.
choices.rationale: Correct: type 3 shows no binding and no response; types 1, 2 and 4 all bind L to the same receptor R yet respond in three different ways, so the response must depend on the cell's downstream components.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell type 4 must lack receptor R, because a cell that binds a ligand but does not respond has no receptor.
choices.rationale: The antibody test shows type 4 has R and it binds L strongly, so the receptor is present and a downstream defect is the more likely cause.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell types 1 and 2 must have different receptors for L, because they respond to L in different ways.
choices.rationale: The stem states that the same receptor protein R is present on both types, so different responses cannot be explained by different receptors.

title: separate ligand binding from cell response using a results table (variant 1)
stem:
A researcher engineers three cell lines to make the same receptor protein, R, at the same level. Each line is exposed to the same concentration of ligand L.
Cell line | Origin | Response to L
1 | liver | breaks down glycogen
2 | neuron | opens an ion channel
3 | skin fibroblast | begins dividing
Which statement best explains why one ligand and one receptor produce three responses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: L enters each cell and decides which genes to turn on, because the response depends on the structure of the ligand.
choices.rationale: L acts by binding the receptor and the stem gives no evidence that it enters the cells, and the same ligand structure gives three different responses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The receptor R changes its structure in each cell line so that it binds a different part of L.
choices.rationale: The same receptor protein is made in all three lines, so no new binding site or structure is needed to explain the differences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cells differ in the number of L molecules that reached them, since only the amount of ligand determines the type of response.
choices.rationale: The same concentration of L was added to every line, so the amount of ligand does not differ among them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each cell line has its own set of signal transduction proteins and effectors, so the same receptor activation leads to different responses.
choices.rationale: Correct: ligand, receptor and ligand concentration are identical in the three lines, so the differences must lie downstream, in each cell's own transduction components and effectors.

title: separate ligand binding from cell response using a results table (variant 2)
stem: Cell line K binds labeled ligand L as strongly as a normal cell line does, yet shows no response. K lacks protein P, a cytoplasmic kinase that normally acts after receptor activation. When the gene for P is added to K, the cells respond to L. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P is the receptor for L, because the response appeared only after P was supplied.
choices.rationale: K already bound L normally before P was added, so a receptor was present, and P is a cytoplasmic kinase and not a surface receptor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The receptor in K works, but the cells lacked a downstream component, P, needed to relay the signal to a response.
choices.rationale: Correct: normal binding shows the receptor and reception step are intact; supplying P restores the response, so the missing piece was a downstream transduction component.

choices.label: C
choices.text: K could not bind L, so the original lack of response was caused by missing ligand binding.
choices.rationale: The stem says K binds L as strongly as a normal line does, so binding was not the problem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: P makes the ligand L, so adding P supplied the signal that K had been missing.
choices.rationale: L was supplied by the researcher in every test, and P is a signaling kinase that does not make ligands.

title: separate ligand binding from cell response using a results table (variant 3)
stem:
Three cell lines were tested with ligand L. In a second test, a membrane-permeable drug that directly activates the downstream kinase of the pathway was added in place of L.
Cell line | Labeled L bound | Response to L | Response to the drug
1 | high | high | high
2 | none | none | high
3 | high | none | none
Which statement is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell line 3 lacks the receptor, since it does not respond to L.
choices.rationale: Line 3 binds L strongly, so the receptor is present, and its failure to respond to the drug as well points downstream.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell line 2 lacks a functional receptor for L but has an intact downstream pathway, while cell line 3 has a receptor but a defect downstream.
choices.rationale: Correct: line 2 does not bind L yet responds when the pathway is activated directly, so reception is the failed step; line 3 binds L but does not respond even to the drug, so the defect lies downstream.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell line 2 has a defect in transduction, since it gives no response to L.
choices.rationale: Line 2 responds to the drug, so its transduction machinery works, and the missing step is binding of L.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell line 1 shows that receptors are never needed, since the drug alone can produce its response.
choices.rationale: The drug is an artificial bypass, and in a normal cell the pathway is turned on by ligand binding to the receptor, as the response of line 1 to L shows.

title: use an experiment to decide receptor location and whether the response needs gene expression
stem: Ligand M is a 30-kDa protein. When M is added to the medium around liver cells, glycogen breakdown begins within 20 seconds. When M is microinjected directly into the cytoplasm of a liver cell, there is no response. The protein-synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide does not change the response to M added outside the cell, but a PKA inhibitor abolishes the response. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: M binds a receptor on the cell surface, and the response is relayed by proteins already in the cytoplasm, such as PKA, without new protein synthesis.
choices.rationale: Correct: a response to outside M but not to injected M places the receptor at the plasma membrane; cycloheximide has no effect, so no new proteins are needed; the PKA inhibitor blocks the response, so PKA relays the signal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: M enters the cell, binds an intracellular receptor, and acts as a transcription factor that produces new proteins within seconds.
choices.rationale: Injecting M into the cytoplasm gave no response, which an intracellular receptor would not predict, and the response needs no new protein synthesis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: M binds a membrane receptor, but the response needs newly synthesized proteins, and cycloheximide did not block them because it acts too slowly.
choices.rationale: The response arises within 20 seconds and cycloheximide had no effect on it, so no newly made proteins are needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: M enters the cell through a channel and directly activates PKA, which then breaks down glycogen.
choices.rationale: If M acted directly on PKA inside the cell, injecting it would have caused a response, and it did not.

title: use an experiment to decide receptor location and whether the response needs gene expression (variant 1)
stem: Hormone S is a small nonpolar molecule. After S is added to cultured cells, the amount of a certain enzyme rises only after 3 hours. The transcription inhibitor actinomycin D prevents the rise. When S is attached to large beads that cannot cross the plasma membrane, there is no response. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: S binds a membrane receptor and activates a kinase cascade that acts within seconds.
choices.rationale: A membrane receptor cascade would respond within seconds to the beads, and the response here is delayed and needs transcription.

choices.label: B
choices.text: S crosses the membrane and binds an intracellular receptor, and the complex changes gene expression, which explains the delay.
choices.rationale: Correct: beads that cannot enter give no response, so S must get inside; actinomycin D blocks the response, so it needs transcription; new mRNA and protein take hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: S acts at the cell surface, because the beads show that S can reach the cell from outside.
choices.rationale: The beads that stay outside the cell give no response, so a surface receptor is not enough for S.

choices.label: D
choices.text: S must first be broken down in the cell to an active form, and transcription is not involved in the delay.
choices.rationale: Actinomycin D blocks the response, so transcription is involved, and the stem gives no evidence of a conversion step.

title: use an experiment to decide receptor location and whether the response needs gene expression (variant 2)
stem: Neurotransmitter N is applied to a muscle fiber and depolarizes the membrane within 5 milliseconds. Replacing the Na⁺ outside the cell with a large ion that cannot pass through channels abolishes the depolarization. Kinase inhibitors and protein-synthesis inhibitors do not change the response. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: N crosses the membrane and binds an intracellular receptor that changes gene expression.
choices.rationale: Gene expression takes much longer than 5 ms and protein-synthesis inhibitors had no effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: N binds a receptor that is itself an ion channel, so binding opens the channel and ions enter, with no second messenger or new gene expression needed.
choices.rationale: Correct: a 5 ms response that needs extracellular Na⁺ but not kinases or new proteins fits a ligand-gated ion channel opened directly by N.

choices.label: C
choices.text: N binds a receptor tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates transcription factors within milliseconds.
choices.rationale: Kinase inhibitors did not change the response, so a kinase-based pathway is not needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: N causes IP₃ to release stored Ca²⁺ from the ER, and the Ca²⁺ then depolarizes the membrane.
choices.rationale: Stored Ca²⁺ release would not depend on the Na⁺ outside the cell, and replacing the Na⁺ abolished the response.

title: use an experiment to decide receptor location and whether the response needs gene expression (variant 3)
stem: In a cell line, ligand L normally raises cAMP and turns on gene G. When drug Z is present, L no longer raises cAMP or turns on gene G, and binding of labeled L drops by 95%. In drug-treated cells, a membrane-permeable cAMP analog turns on gene G strongly. Which stage of signaling does Z most likely block?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transduction, because Z prevents the cell from making cAMP after L binds.
choices.rationale: Z reduces the binding of L, so reception fails first, and the cell can still respond to cAMP, so making cAMP is not shown to be the blocked step.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The response, because Z stops gene G from being turned on even when cAMP is high.
choices.rationale: Gene G turns on strongly when cAMP analog is added, so the response step is intact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reception, because Z stops L from binding its receptor, while transduction and the response are intact.
choices.rationale: Correct: Z cuts labeled L binding by 95% (reception), and cAMP analog restores gene G expression (transduction after cAMP and the response work).

choices.label: D
choices.text: All three stages, because Z prevented L from turning on gene G.
choices.rationale: The cAMP analog restores the response, so the later stages work and only reception is shown to be blocked.

title: calculate how amplification through a cascade scales output when one step changes
stem: In a cell, each hormone-bound receptor activates 20 G proteins. Each active G protein activates one adenylyl cyclase, and each activated adenylyl cyclase makes 50 cAMP molecules before it is inactivated. A mutation lowers the number of G proteins activated per hormone-bound receptor from 20 to 5; all other steps are unchanged. If 300 receptors bind hormone, which statement describes the cAMP produced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 75,000 cAMP molecules, one fourth of the normal amount, because a smaller yield at the first step is carried through the later multiplying steps.
choices.rationale: Correct: normal output is 300 × 20 × 50 = 300,000 cAMP; with the mutation it is 300 × 5 × 50 = 75,000, which is one fourth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 150,000 cAMP molecules, half of the normal amount, because the mutation removes half of the G proteins.
choices.rationale: Going from 20 to 5 G proteins is a fourfold decrease and not a twofold decrease, so the output falls to one fourth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1,500 cAMP molecules, because only the 5 G proteins per receptor make cAMP.
choices.rationale: 300 × 5 = 1,500 counts activated G proteins and leaves out the 50 cAMP made by each adenylyl cyclase.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 300,000 cAMP molecules, unchanged, because the later steps of the cascade make up for the loss.
choices.rationale: The later steps only multiply what they receive and cannot restore a lower number of activated G proteins.

title: calculate how amplification through a cascade scales output when one step changes (variant 1)
stem: In a kinase cascade, each active kinase K1 activates 10 molecules of K2, each active K2 activates 10 molecules of K3, and each active K3 phosphorylates 10 molecules of a transcription factor. A drug changes K2 so that each active K2 activates only 5 K3 molecules. If 40 K1 molecules are active, which statement describes the number of phosphorylated transcription factor molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 40,000, unchanged, because the later step adds 10 for each K3 and so corrects the loss.
choices.rationale: Each step only multiplies the number it receives, so fewer K3 means fewer phosphorylated factors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 10,000, one fourth of normal, because the change at the second step affects two steps.
choices.rationale: Only one step changed and it was halved from 10 to 5, so the output halves and does not fall to a quarter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 200, because only the 5 K3 per K2 matter for the final amount.
choices.rationale: 40 × 5 = 200 ignores the multiplication by the other steps of the cascade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 20,000, half of the normal 40,000, because halving the output of one step halves the final output.
choices.rationale: Correct: normal is 40 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 40,000; with the drug it is 40 × 10 × 5 × 10 = 20,000, which is half.

title: calculate how amplification through a cascade scales output when one step changes (variant 2)
stem: Two hypothetical pathways are compared. In pathway X, each of 100 ligand-bound receptors directly activates one transcription factor. In pathway Y, each of 100 ligand-bound receptors activates 5 kinase molecules, and each kinase activates 5 transcription factors. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pathway Y activates 500 transcription factors, because each receptor activates 5 molecules.
choices.rationale: 100 × 5 = 500 counts only the first step and leaves out the 5 transcription factors activated by each kinase.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pathway Y activates 1,000 transcription factors, because the 5 and 5 are added at each receptor.
choices.rationale: The amplification at the steps is multiplied (5 × 5 = 25 per receptor), not added (5 + 5 = 10).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pathway Y activates 2,500 transcription factors, which is 25 times as many as pathway X, because each step multiplies the signal.
choices.rationale: Correct: pathway X gives 100; pathway Y gives 100 × 5 × 5 = 2,500, which is 25 times as large.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pathway X and Y activate the same number, because the number of receptors sets the number of active transcription factors.
choices.rationale: The number of receptors is the same, but extra steps with several targets per enzyme give a larger output in Y.

title: calculate how amplification through a cascade scales output when one step changes (variant 3)
stem:
A researcher measures how much of a cell's maximum response is produced when different fractions of its receptors are occupied by ligand.
Receptors occupied | Response (percent of maximum)
5% | 40%
20% | 85%
100% | 100%
Which interpretation is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The response is directly proportional to the fraction of receptors occupied, so 5% occupancy gives 5% of the maximum.
choices.rationale: The data show 5% occupancy giving 40% of the maximum, which is not proportional.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Occupancy above 20% harms the cell, so the response levels off.
choices.rationale: The response levels off because the downstream machinery nears its maximum, and the data give no sign of damage to the cell.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Occupying a small fraction of the receptors gives a large share of the maximum response, as expected when downstream steps amplify the signal.
choices.rationale: Correct: 5% occupancy yields 40% of the maximum, a much larger fraction than the occupancy, which is the signature of amplification after reception.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ligand must enter the cell to produce a response, so the limit on the response is how fast the ligand is transported.
choices.rationale: The experiment concerns receptor occupancy and the stem gives no evidence that the ligand enters the cell or that transport limits the response.

title: predict effect of a constitutively active component and of blocking different steps
stem: In a signaling pathway, growth factor binding activates receptor R, which activates Ras, then Raf, then MEK, then ERK. Active ERK turns on genes for cell proliferation. A cell line has a mutation that keeps Raf active even without input from Ras. The cells are grown with no growth factor. Which result is predicted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The proliferation genes are on, and a MEK inhibitor turns them off, but an antibody that blocks receptor R does not.
choices.rationale: Correct: Raf is downstream of the receptor and Ras, so its constant activity keeps MEK and ERK active without ligand; blocking the receptor acts upstream of the mutation and has no effect, but blocking MEK downstream of it cuts the signal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proliferation genes stay off until growth factor is added, because Raf cannot act without Ras.
choices.rationale: The mutation makes Raf active without Ras, so the downstream steps proceed without growth factor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proliferation genes are on, and an antibody that blocks receptor R turns them off.
choices.rationale: The receptor acts upstream of Raf, and blocking it cannot switch off a Raf that is active without any input.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proliferation genes are on, and a MEK inhibitor does not turn them off, because active Raf can bypass MEK.
choices.rationale: In this pathway Raf activates ERK only through MEK, so blocking MEK stops the signal.

title: predict effect of a constitutively active component and of blocking different steps (variant 1)
stem: In intestinal cells, a hormone binds a receptor that activates Gs, which activates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP. cAMP activates PKA, and PKA triggers chloride secretion. Cholera toxin modifies Gs so that it cannot break down its bound GTP and stays active. Cells are treated with the toxin and no hormone. Which result is predicted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cAMP stays high, and a receptor antagonist lowers it, because the receptor must keep activating Gs.
choices.rationale: The receptor acts upstream of Gs, and Gs is already locked in its active state, so blocking the receptor does not lower cAMP.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cAMP stays low until the hormone is added, because Gs cannot work without the receptor.
choices.rationale: Toxin-modified Gs stays active even with no hormone, so cAMP does not wait for the hormone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: cAMP stays high, but a PKA inhibitor has no effect on secretion, because cAMP acts independently of PKA.
choices.rationale: In this pathway cAMP signals through PKA, so a PKA inhibitor blocks the response to high cAMP.

choices.label: D
choices.text: cAMP stays high and chloride secretion continues, a receptor antagonist does not reduce it, and a PKA inhibitor does.
choices.rationale: Correct: a Gs that cannot turn itself off keeps adenylyl cyclase active without receptor input; PKA lies downstream of cAMP, so only a PKA inhibitor can stop the secretion.

title: predict effect of a constitutively active component and of blocking different steps (variant 2)
stem: In a pathway, ligand L activates receptor R. R activates kinase K1, and K1's only target is kinase K2. K2 phosphorylates transcription factor TF, which turns on gene G. A cell line has no functional K2 enzyme (the K2 protein is made but has no catalytic activity). Cells are treated with L. Which result is predicted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: R is not activated, because the cell detects the missing K2 and blocks the receptor.
choices.rationale: The receptor is activated by the ligand upstream of K2, and the stem gives no mechanism that blocks it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: K1 is not activated either, because the pathway shuts off all steps when one step fails.
choices.rationale: K1 acts upstream of K2 and is activated normally, since a defect at one step does not stop the earlier steps.

choices.label: C
choices.text: R and K1 are activated as usual, but TF is not phosphorylated and gene G stays off.
choices.rationale: Correct: ligand binding activates R, which activates K1 (both upstream of the defect), but K2 cannot pass the signal to TF, and K1's only target is K2, so gene G remains off.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene G turns on at the normal level, because K1 can phosphorylate TF directly.
choices.rationale: The stem states that K1 acts only on K2, so no other route to TF exists.

title: predict effect of a constitutively active component and of blocking different steps (variant 3)
stem: A receptor tyrosine kinase is normally activated when ligand binding makes two receptor molecules pair and phosphorylate each other, which then switches on a downstream kinase pathway. A cell line has a mutation that makes receptor molecules pair with each other even when no ligand is bound. Which result is predicted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pathway is on without ligand, an inhibitor that blocks ligand binding has no effect, and an inhibitor of the receptor's kinase domain turns it off.
choices.rationale: Correct: the mutation bypasses the ligand step, so receptor phosphorylation and the downstream pathway run without ligand; only blocking the kinase activity of the receptor, or a downstream step, can stop it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The downstream pathway stays off until ligand is added, because the receptors need ligand for any activity.
choices.rationale: The mutation makes receptors pair without ligand, so the receptors have activity without it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pathway is on only briefly, because unpaired receptors quickly return to the ligand-bound form.
choices.rationale: The stem gives no mechanism for turning off the paired receptors, and pairing is held by the mutation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pathway is on, and an inhibitor that blocks ligand binding turns it off.
choices.rationale: The receptors are already paired and active, so blocking the binding of ligand cannot reverse that.

title: work out the order of proteins in a pathway from rescue experiments
stem:
Three proteins, X, Y and Z, act in a single linear pathway between a receptor and a gene response. Researchers made cell lines that each lack one protein, then tested whether adding a constitutively active form of another protein (CA) turns on the response when no ligand is present.
Cell line | Response to ligand | CA-X, no ligand | CA-Y, no ligand | CA-Z, no ligand
Lacks X | none | not tested | response | no response
Lacks Y | none | no response | not tested | no response
Lacks Z | none | response | response | not tested
Which order of action, from the receptor to the response, fits the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X, then Y, then Z.
choices.rationale: If X came first, CA-Z and CA-Y would rescue the line lacking X, and CA-Z did not rescue it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Z, then Y, then X.
choices.rationale: If Y came before X, CA-X would rescue the line lacking Y, and it did not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Y, then X, then Z.
choices.rationale: If Y came first, CA-X would rescue a line lacking Y, and the table shows it did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Z, then X, then Y.
choices.rationale: Correct: an active protein can rescue only a line that lacks something upstream of it. Lines lacking Z are rescued by both CA-X and CA-Y, so Z is first. A line lacking X is rescued by CA-Y but not CA-Z, so Y is after X. The line lacking Y is rescued by neither, so Y is last.

title: work out the order of proteins in a pathway from rescue experiments (variant 1)
stem:
A pathway in a cell has three kinases, KA, KB and KC. After the ligand is added, the researchers add a drug that blocks one kinase at a time and measure which kinases become phosphorylated (active).
Drug target | KA phosphorylated | KB phosphorylated | KC phosphorylated
KA blocked | no | no | no
KB blocked | yes | no | no
KC blocked | yes | yes | no
Which order of action fits the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: KC, then KB, then KA.
choices.rationale: If KC acted first, blocking KC would stop KB and KA, but KA and KB were phosphorylated with KC blocked.

choices.label: B
choices.text: KB, then KA, then KC.
choices.rationale: If KB acted before KA, blocking KB would stop KA, and KA was still phosphorylated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The three kinases act in parallel, each one switched on directly by the receptor.
choices.rationale: In a parallel pathway, blocking one kinase would leave the others active, and blocking KA stopped all three.

choices.label: D
choices.text: KA, then KB, then KC.
choices.rationale: Correct: blocking a kinase prevents activation of the kinases downstream of it but not those upstream; blocking KA stops all three, blocking KB stops KB and KC, and blocking KC stops only KC.

title: work out the order of proteins in a pathway from rescue experiments (variant 2)
stem:
Four proteins, F, G, H and J, act in a linear pathway from a receptor to a gene response. Each cell line lacks one protein. In each line, no ligand is given and a constitutively active form of one of the other proteins is added.
Cell line | Active forms that turn on the response
Lacks F | H, J, G
Lacks G | none
Lacks H | J, G
Lacks J | G
Which order of action, from the receptor to the response, fits the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: J, then H, then F, then G.
choices.rationale: If J came first, active J would not rescue the line lacking H, but it did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: G, then J, then H, then F.
choices.rationale: If G came first, active G would not rescue lines lacking J and H and F, but it rescued all three.

choices.label: C
choices.text: F, then H, then J, then G.
choices.rationale: Correct: the line lacking G is not rescued, so G is last. The line lacking F is rescued by all three others, so F is first. The line lacking H is rescued by J and G but not F, so H comes after F and before J. The line lacking J is rescued only by G, so J comes after H and before G.

choices.label: D
choices.text: F, then J, then H, then G.
choices.rationale: If J came before H, active J would not rescue the line lacking H, and the table shows it did.

title: work out the order of proteins in a pathway from rescue experiments (variant 3)
stem: After a hormone is added to cells, three proteins, T, S and U, become phosphorylated: T at 10 seconds, S at 30 seconds, and U at 60 seconds. When an inhibitor of T is added before the hormone, neither S nor U is phosphorylated. When an inhibitor of U is added before the hormone, T and S are still phosphorylated. Which order of action fits the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: U, then S, then T.
choices.rationale: If U acted first, blocking U would prevent T and S from being phosphorylated, and they were.

choices.label: B
choices.text: S, then T, then U.
choices.rationale: If S acted before T, blocking T would not stop S, and it did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: T, then S, then U.
choices.rationale: Correct: blocking T prevents S and U, so T is first; blocking U leaves T and S active, so U is not upstream of them; the timing agrees with T, S, U.

choices.label: D
choices.text: T and U act separately, and S acts after both.
choices.rationale: Blocking T stopped both S and U, so U depends on T and does not act separately.

title: predict hormone levels when a negative feedback loop is interrupted at one step
stem: In healthy people, the pituitary hormone ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol, and cortisol acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary to reduce ACTH release. A patient takes a drug that blocks an enzyme the adrenal cortex needs to make cortisol. The adrenal cortex and pituitary otherwise work normally. Which pattern of blood hormone levels is expected after two weeks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cortisol low and ACTH high, because less cortisol means less inhibition of ACTH release.
choices.rationale: Correct: the drug lowers cortisol; with less negative feedback on the pituitary, ACTH release rises and stays high because the adrenal cortex cannot make cortisol to turn it off.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol low and ACTH low, because low cortisol reduces the stimulus for ACTH release.
choices.rationale: This treats the loop as positive feedback, but cortisol inhibits ACTH release, so a drop in cortisol raises ACTH.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cortisol low and ACTH normal, because cortisol does not regulate ACTH release.
choices.rationale: The stem states that cortisol acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary to reduce ACTH, so ACTH release is regulated by cortisol.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cortisol normal and ACTH normal, because negative feedback always returns hormone levels to normal whatever the drug.
choices.rationale: Feedback can correct a variable only if the components work, and the drug blocks cortisol synthesis so the loop cannot restore cortisol.

title: predict hormone levels when a negative feedback loop is interrupted at one step (variant 1)
stem: A patient takes a high dose of prednisone, a drug that acts like cortisol, for several months. Normally, ACTH from the pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to make cortisol, and cortisol reduces ACTH release. Which change in the patient's own ACTH release and adrenal cortex is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ACTH release rises and the adrenal cortex enlarges, because the body needs to make more cortisol.
choices.rationale: The drug acts like cortisol, so it adds inhibition and ACTH falls and does not rise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: ACTH release is unchanged and the adrenal cortex is unchanged, because a drug cannot affect the loop.
choices.rationale: Prednisone acts as cortisol would and engages the same feedback on the pituitary, so ACTH release changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: ACTH release falls and the adrenal cortex enlarges, because less ACTH makes the adrenal cortex grow.
choices.rationale: The adrenal cortex depends on ACTH for stimulation, so less ACTH leads to shrinkage and not growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: ACTH release falls and the adrenal cortex shrinks, because the drug acts like cortisol and the adrenal cortex gets less stimulation.
choices.rationale: Correct: prednisone supplies the negative feedback signal, so ACTH release falls; with little ACTH stimulation the adrenal cortex makes less cortisol and shrinks.

title: predict hormone levels when a negative feedback loop is interrupted at one step (variant 2)
stem: Parathyroid cells release PTH when blood Ca²⁺ is low. PTH raises blood Ca²⁺. A calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells detects high blood Ca²⁺ and reduces PTH release. A patient has a mutation that makes the receptor insensitive to Ca²⁺. Which pattern is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PTH low and blood Ca²⁺ low, because the cells cannot sense calcium.
choices.rationale: Without the sensor, the signal that reduces PTH is lost, so PTH release continues and does not fall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: PTH high and blood Ca²⁺ high, because the cells do not detect high Ca²⁺ and keep releasing PTH.
choices.rationale: Correct: with the sensor unable to detect high Ca²⁺, the inhibition of PTH release is lost, so PTH stays high and keeps raising blood Ca²⁺.

choices.label: C
choices.text: PTH normal and blood Ca²⁺ normal, because other organs make up for the missing sensor.
choices.rationale: The stem describes no compensating mechanism, and the lost feedback leaves PTH unchecked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: PTH high and blood Ca²⁺ low, because the cells release PTH but it cannot act.
choices.rationale: PTH acts normally in this patient and raises blood Ca²⁺, so the calcium level rises and does not stay low.

title: predict hormone levels when a negative feedback loop is interrupted at one step (variant 3)
stem: In a bacterium, enzyme 1 begins a pathway that makes end product Z. Z normally binds an allosteric site on enzyme 1 and inhibits it. A mutant enzyme 1 has a normal active site but can no longer bind Z. Compared with the normal bacterium, which result is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Z levels are lower in the mutant, because the mutant enzyme has lost activity.
choices.rationale: The active site is normal, so the enzyme is not less active, and only the inhibition by Z is gone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Z levels are the same, because the cell breaks down any extra Z.
choices.rationale: The stem gives no mechanism that removes extra Z, and without feedback the pathway keeps running.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Z levels are lower in the mutant, because the loss of feedback inhibition acts as positive feedback.
choices.rationale: Losing negative feedback does not turn it into positive feedback, and the result is overproduction and not underproduction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Z levels are higher in the mutant, because enzyme 1 stays active when Z accumulates.
choices.rationale: Correct: the active site works but the allosteric inhibition is lost, so enzyme 1 keeps making product however much Z is present, and Z accumulates.

title: evaluate a student's claim about negative versus positive feedback
stem: During labor, the baby's head presses on the cervix, stretch receptors signal the hypothalamus, and the posterior pituitary releases oxytocin. Oxytocin makes the uterine muscle contract more strongly, which presses the head harder on the cervix. After delivery the cervix is no longer stretched and oxytocin release falls. A student claims: "This is negative feedback, because the process stops by itself at the end." Which evaluation is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is wrong: the contractions increase the stimulus that raises oxytocin, which is positive feedback, and the loop ends only because delivery removes the stimulus.
choices.rationale: Correct: the output (stronger contraction) increases the input (cervical stretch), so the loop amplifies the change; negative feedback would reduce it. The loop ends because an outside event, delivery, removes the stimulus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because any process that ends on its own is negative feedback.
choices.rationale: Ending does not define negative feedback, since the type depends on whether the output opposes or amplifies the change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is wrong, because hormones can take part only in positive feedback loops.
choices.rationale: Many hormone loops, such as ACTH and cortisol, are negative feedback, so hormones are not limited to positive loops.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is correct, because negative feedback means the response is helpful to the organism.
choices.rationale: Whether feedback is helpful does not define its type, and positive feedback can be helpful, as here.

title: evaluate a student's claim about negative versus positive feedback (variant 1)
stem: In a neuron, depolarization opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, Na⁺ entry depolarizes the membrane further, and that opens more Na⁺ channels. Within about a millisecond, the channels inactivate and K⁺ channels open, which returns the membrane toward its resting value. A student claims: "Cells must keep conditions steady, so a positive feedback loop cannot occur inside a cell." Which evaluation is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because positive feedback always damages cells.
choices.rationale: Positive feedback is a normal part of the nerve impulse and is not damaging here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is wrong: the opening of Na⁺ channels is positive feedback that rapidly amplifies the depolarization, and it is brief and is ended by channel inactivation.
choices.rationale: Correct: depolarization opening more channels that cause more depolarization is amplification (positive feedback); other processes, inactivation and K⁺ channels, end it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is correct, because the Na⁺ channel step must be negative feedback, since the membrane returns to rest.
choices.rationale: The return to rest is caused by other events, channel inactivation and K⁺ channels, while the Na⁺ channel step itself amplifies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is wrong, because Na⁺ channel opening is negative feedback that keeps the membrane near its set point.
choices.rationale: Negative feedback reduces a change, and Na⁺ channel opening increases the depolarization.

title: evaluate a student's claim about negative versus positive feedback (variant 2)
stem: A ripening apple releases ethylene gas. Ethylene triggers cells in the apple, and in nearby apples, to make more ethylene, so the ethylene concentration rises rapidly. A student claims: "A feedback loop must keep a variable steady, so this cannot be a feedback loop at all." Which evaluation is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because ethylene production keeps changing and so there is no feedback.
choices.rationale: Feedback means the output influences its own production, and ethylene production is controlled by ethylene, so feedback is present.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because only negative feedback loops count as feedback.
choices.rationale: Positive feedback loops are feedback too, and they amplify a change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is wrong, because this is negative feedback with a set point at a very high ethylene level.
choices.rationale: No set point is being defended, and the ethylene level keeps rising instead of returning to a value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is wrong: this is a positive feedback loop, in which the output increases the stimulus and drives the variable further from its starting value.
choices.rationale: Correct: ethylene stimulates more ethylene, so the output amplifies the change; keeping a variable near a set point describes negative feedback only.

title: evaluate a student's claim about negative versus positive feedback (variant 3)
stem: When body temperature rises above 37°C, the sweat rate increases. As the sweat evaporates, body temperature falls back toward 37°C and the sweat rate decreases. A student claims: "This is positive feedback, because sweat rate went up when the temperature went up." Which evaluation is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is correct, because the response and the stimulus changed in the same direction.
choices.rationale: The direction in which the stimulus and the response change does not decide the type, and the effect of the response on the stimulus does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is correct, because sweating is an amplified response.
choices.rationale: A large response is not what defines positive feedback, since the response here reduces the temperature rise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is wrong: sweating opposes the rise in temperature and returns it toward the set point, which is negative feedback.
choices.rationale: Correct: the type of feedback depends on the effect of the response on the original change; here the response counteracts the change, which is negative feedback.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim is wrong, because feedback loops involve hormones and sweating is controlled by nerves.
choices.rationale: Feedback loops are not limited to hormones, and nervous and other control systems use feedback too.

title: estimate time in a phase from counts of cells in a sample
stem: A researcher examines 200 cells from a growing root tip under the microscope. The cell cycle in this tissue lasts 24 hours. Counts: interphase 160, prophase 16, metaphase 8, anaphase 6, telophase 10. About how long does a cell spend in metaphase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 0.04 hours, because 8 of 200 cells are in metaphase.
choices.rationale: 0.04 is the fraction of cells and it has to be multiplied by the 24-hour cycle to give hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1.9 hours, because 8 of every 100 cells are in metaphase.
choices.rationale: 8 of 200 cells is 4 of every 100 cells and not 8 of every 100.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 4.8 hours, because 8 of the 40 dividing cells are in metaphase.
choices.rationale: The share of the 40 dividing cells (20%) gives the fraction of mitosis, and the denominator must be all 200 cells and the cycle length.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 1.0 hour, because 8/200 of the cells are in metaphase and the cycle is 24 hours long.
choices.rationale: Correct: the fraction of cells in a phase is the fraction of the cycle spent in it: 8/200 = 0.04, and 0.04 × 24 h = 0.96 h, about 1 hour.

title: estimate time in a phase from counts of cells in a sample (variant 1)
stem: An onion root tip sample of 300 cells is counted. The cell cycle lasts 20 hours. Counts: interphase 240, prophase 30, metaphase 12, anaphase 6, telophase 12. About how long does a cell spend in mitosis (prophase through telophase)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 0.2 hours, because 60 of 300 cells are in mitosis.
choices.rationale: 60/300 = 0.2 is a fraction and must be multiplied by the 20-hour cycle to give hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5 hours, because 60 cells in mitosis divided by 240 cells in interphase is 25% of 20 hours.
choices.rationale: The denominator must be all 300 cells, and using only the 240 interphase cells gives the wrong fraction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 4 hours, because 60 of the 300 cells are in mitosis, which is 20% of the 20-hour cycle.
choices.rationale: Correct: mitotic cells are 30 + 12 + 6 + 12 = 60 of 300, which is 20%, and 0.20 × 20 h = 4 h.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 16 hours, because most of the cells are in the stage with no visible chromosomes.
choices.rationale: 16 hours is the time in interphase, and the question asks about mitosis.

title: estimate time in a phase from counts of cells in a sample (variant 2)
stem: In a culture of dividing cells, 5% of the cells are in metaphase at any moment, and metaphase lasts 30 minutes. What is the length of the whole cell cycle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2.5 hours, because 0.5 hours is multiplied by 5.
choices.rationale: Multiplying 0.5 by 5 does not match the proportion; the phase time is the fraction times the cycle, so the cycle is the phase time divided by the fraction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.025 hours, because 0.5 hours is multiplied by 0.05.
choices.rationale: Multiplying by the fraction goes the wrong way, because it gives a time shorter than metaphase itself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 9.5 hours, because the 0.5 hours of metaphase is subtracted from the 10-hour cycle.
choices.rationale: 9.5 hours is the cycle without metaphase and does not equal the full cycle time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 10 hours, because 0.5 hours is 5% of the cycle length.
choices.rationale: Correct: if metaphase is 5% of the cycle and lasts 0.5 h, the cycle is 0.5 / 0.05 = 10 h.

title: estimate time in a phase from counts of cells in a sample (variant 3)
stem:
A researcher counts 200 cells from a culture before and after 6 hours of treatment with a drug.
Phase | Before drug | After 6 hours of drug
Interphase | 190 | 70
Prophase | 4 | 8
Metaphase | 3 | 118
Anaphase | 1 | 1
Telophase | 2 | 3
Which interpretation is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The drug speeds up mitosis, because far more cells are in mitosis after treatment.
choices.rationale: If mitosis were faster, fewer cells would be caught in mitosis at a moment, and metaphase would not hold most of them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug blocks the move from metaphase to anaphase, so cells that enter mitosis pile up in metaphase.
choices.rationale: Correct: metaphase cells rise from 3 to 118 while anaphase and telophase stay near 1 to 3, so cells reach metaphase and cannot go on.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug stops cells from entering mitosis, because the number of interphase cells fell.
choices.rationale: Interphase cells fell because cells entered mitosis and stayed in it, so entry is not blocked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug blocks cytokinesis, because cells accumulate at the end of mitosis.
choices.rationale: Telophase cells did not accumulate (3 cells), so the block comes before telophase.

title: infer cell-cycle arrest point from DNA content distribution
stem:
A cultured cell line has 3.0 pg of DNA per cell in G1 and 6.0 pg after DNA replication is complete, until the cell divides. Flow cytometry measures DNA per cell.
Sample | Cells at 3.0 pg | Cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg | Cells at 6.0 pg
Untreated | 52% | 18% | 30%
24 hours with drug D | 6% | 9% | 85%
Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug D arrests cells in G1, before DNA replication begins.
choices.rationale: A G1 arrest would leave most cells at 3.0 pg, and only 6% are there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug D arrests cells during S phase, partway through DNA replication.
choices.rationale: An S-phase arrest would leave most cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg, and only 9% are there.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug D lets cells replicate their DNA but arrests them in G2 or mitosis, before the cell divides.
choices.rationale: Correct: most treated cells hold 6.0 pg, so they have completed S phase, and few are at 3.0 pg or in between; they stay at 6.0 pg until division, so they are arrested in G2 or M.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug D makes cells leave the cycle and enter G0, in which they hold 6.0 pg of DNA.
choices.rationale: Cells in G0 have not replicated their DNA and would hold 3.0 pg.

title: infer cell-cycle arrest point from DNA content distribution (variant 1)
stem:
A haploid yeast strain has a temperature-sensitive mutation in a gene. DNA content is measured in relative units (1 unit in G1, 2 units after replication).
Sample | Cells at 1 unit | Cells between 1 and 2 units | Cells at 2 units
Permissive temperature | 50% | 20% | 30%
4 hours at restrictive temperature | 92% | 5% | 3%
Which conclusion is best supported about the mutated gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gene product is needed to move from G1 into DNA replication.
choices.rationale: Correct: nearly all mutant cells end up at 1 unit, so they never start DNA replication.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gene product is needed to complete DNA replication during S phase.
choices.rationale: A defect in completing S phase would leave many cells between 1 and 2 units, and only 5% are there.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gene product is needed to carry out mitosis, so cells pile up with replicated DNA.
choices.rationale: A defect in mitosis would leave cells at 2 units, and only 3% are there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gene product is needed for cytokinesis, so cells pile up with two nuclei and 2 units of DNA.
choices.rationale: A cytokinesis defect would also leave cells at 2 units or more, and the cells are at 1 unit.

title: infer cell-cycle arrest point from DNA content distribution (variant 2)
stem: A drug that blocks nucleotide synthesis is added to cultured cells that hold 3.0 pg of DNA in G1 and 6.0 pg after replication. After 12 hours, flow cytometry shows 8% of cells at 3.0 pg, 87% between 3.0 and 6.0 pg, and 5% at 6.0 pg. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA replication began but cannot be completed, so most cells are stuck partway through S phase.
choices.rationale: Correct: most cells hold intermediate amounts of DNA, so they started to copy their DNA but did not finish, which fits blocked nucleotide synthesis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cells are arrested in G1, before replication starts.
choices.rationale: Cells in G1 hold 3.0 pg, and only 8% are there.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cells are arrested in G2, after replication is complete.
choices.rationale: Cells in G2 hold 6.0 pg, and only 5% are there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cells are arrested in mitosis, before the cells divide.
choices.rationale: Cells in mitosis also hold 6.0 pg, so the data do not show a mitotic arrest.

title: infer cell-cycle arrest point from DNA content distribution (variant 3)
stem: Cells are kept in medium without serum for 4 days. Flow cytometry shows 93% of the cells at 3.0 pg of DNA (the amount in G1 before replication). Twenty hours after serum is added, 40% of the cells are at 3.0 pg, 35% are between 3.0 and 6.0 pg, and 25% are at 6.0 pg. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The starved cells were arrested before DNA replication (in G1 or G0), and serum let them re-enter the cycle, replicate DNA and move on.
choices.rationale: Correct: starved cells hold only 3.0 pg, so they are in G1 or G0; after serum, many cells hold intermediate or 6.0 pg amounts, which means DNA replication occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The starved cells were arrested in G2, and serum made them divide and enter G1.
choices.rationale: Cells arrested in G2 would hold 6.0 pg, and the starved cells held 3.0 pg.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum blocks DNA replication, so the cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg are damaged.
choices.rationale: Cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg are copying their DNA, which shows replication happened and was not blocked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum makes cells skip S phase and go directly into mitosis.
choices.rationale: Cells that skip S would not gain DNA, and many cells now have more than 3.0 pg.

title: predict effect of nondegradable cyclin using cyclin and CDK dynamics
stem: In dividing cells, the concentration of the kinase CDK1 stays constant. Cyclin B accumulates during G2, peaks at metaphase, and falls sharply at anaphase. CDK1 kinase activity rises and falls with the amount of cyclin B. A mutant cyclin B cannot be degraded. Which outcome is most likely in cells that make only the mutant cyclin B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cells never enter mitosis, because CDK1 cannot be activated by the mutant cyclin.
choices.rationale: The mutant cyclin builds up like the normal one and activates CDK1, so entry into mitosis is not blocked.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cells enter mitosis normally but cannot complete it, because CDK1 activity stays high after anaphase.
choices.rationale: Correct: cyclin B rises normally, so CDK1 activates and the cells enter mitosis; without degradation of cyclin B, CDK1 stays active and mitosis cannot be completed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cells skip mitosis and begin another round of DNA replication, because cyclin B is present.
choices.rationale: High cyclin B and CDK1 activity keep cells in mitosis, and they do not move into a new round of replication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cells divide normally, because the amount of CDK1 and not the amount of cyclin sets the timing.
choices.rationale: CDK1 is constant, and its activity depends on cyclin B, so the cyclin level controls timing.

title: predict effect of nondegradable cyclin using cyclin and CDK dynamics (variant 1)
stem:
A researcher measures a cell population through one cell cycle.
Stage | CDK1 protein (relative) | Cyclin B (relative) | CDK1 kinase activity (relative)
G1 | 1.0 | 0.1 | 0.1
S | 1.0 | 0.2 | 0.2
G2 | 1.0 | 0.8 | 0.7
Metaphase | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0
After anaphase | 1.0 | 0.1 | 0.1
Which statement best explains why kinase activity changes even though the amount of CDK1 stays the same?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CDK1 is active only when it is bound to cyclin B, so kinase activity follows the cyclin B level.
choices.rationale: Correct: CDK1 protein is constant at 1.0, while kinase activity tracks the cyclin B column, showing that CDK1 depends on cyclin binding for activity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CDK1 is made and degraded in each cycle, so its amount follows the activity.
choices.rationale: The table shows CDK1 at 1.0 at every stage, so its amount does not change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CDK1 activity is independent of cyclin B, and the matching pattern is a coincidence.
choices.rationale: Activity tracks cyclin B closely at every stage, which is not a coincidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cyclin B is an enzyme that phosphorylates targets by itself, and CDK1 only holds it in place.
choices.rationale: Cyclins have no kinase activity of their own, and the kinase is the CDK that cyclin binding activates.

title: predict effect of nondegradable cyclin using cyclin and CDK dynamics (variant 2)
stem: After DNA damage, a cell makes large amounts of p21, a protein that binds and inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes needed to pass from G1 into S phase. Which result is predicted in the cells with high p21?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CDK activity rises and the cells enter S phase faster.
choices.rationale: P21 is an inhibitor, so CDK activity falls and the cells do not enter S phase faster.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CDK activity falls, and the cells arrest in G2 after DNA replication.
choices.rationale: The inhibited complexes act at the G1 to S transition, so cells stop before they replicate DNA, and not after.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CDK activity falls, and the cells arrest in G1 before DNA replication begins.
choices.rationale: Correct: p21 inhibits the cyclin-CDK complexes needed for the G1 to S transition, so the cells stop in G1 before replication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CDK activity is unchanged, because inhibitors act only on cyclin synthesis.
choices.rationale: P21 binds the cyclin-CDK complexes and lowers their activity directly, so activity does change.

title: predict effect of nondegradable cyclin using cyclin and CDK dynamics (variant 3)
stem: In a classic experiment, researchers fused cells at different stages of the cell cycle. When a G1 cell was fused to a cell in S phase, the G1 nucleus began to replicate DNA early. When a G1 cell was fused to a cell in M phase, the G1 nucleus condensed its chromosomes. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cytoplasm of S-phase and M-phase cells contains diffusible regulators that can push a nucleus from G1 into that phase.
choices.rationale: Correct: the G1 nucleus changes behavior after it is exposed to the cytoplasm of the fused partner, which shows that diffusible factors in S and M cells trigger replication and mitosis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The stage of a cell is set only by the amount of DNA in its nucleus, with no role for cytoplasmic factors.
choices.rationale: A G1 nucleus with unreplicated DNA began to replicate and to condense after fusion, so DNA amount alone does not set the stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regulators of the cell cycle stay inside the nucleus and cannot move between cells.
choices.rationale: The factors acted across the fused cytoplasm, so they were able to move from one nucleus to another.

choices.label: D
choices.text: G1 nuclei hold inhibitors that stop S and M phase from starting.
choices.rationale: The G1 nucleus responded to the signals from the partner cell, so it was not blocking S and M phase.

title: link loss of a checkpoint protein to cell-cycle behavior using data
stem:
Cells with normal p53 (WT) and cells with a mutated p53 gene are grown, and half of each group is exposed to UV light that damages DNA. Twenty-four hours later, researchers measure the percent of cells in G1 and S and the level of p21 protein.
Cells | UV | In G1 | In S | p21 level
WT | no | 60% | 30% | low
WT | yes | 90% | 4% | high
Mutated p53 | no | 60% | 30% | low
Mutated p53 | yes | 58% | 31% | low
Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: p53 speeds up the cell cycle, because WT cells have more cells in G1.
choices.rationale: Undamaged WT and mutated cells have the same percent in G1, so p53 does not change cycle speed on its own.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutated cells are in G0 after UV exposure, because they show no change.
choices.rationale: Cells in G0 would not be cycling, and 31% of the mutated cells are in S, so they keep dividing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After DNA damage, p53 raises p21 and holds cells in G1; without p53, damaged cells continue into S phase.
choices.rationale: Correct: without UV the two groups are the same, so p53 does not change the cycle by itself; after UV, only the WT cells raise p21 and arrest in G1, while mutated cells keep going into S phase.

choices.label: D
choices.text: p53 repairs the UV damage directly, which allows the WT cells to enter S phase.
choices.rationale: WT cells enter S phase far less after UV (4% against 30%), so they are held back and not helped to enter, and the data do not show repair.

title: link loss of a checkpoint protein to cell-cycle behavior using data (variant 1)
stem: The Rb protein binds the transcription factor E2F in G1 and prevents E2F from turning on S-phase genes. Growth factor signaling leads to phosphorylation of Rb, which releases E2F. A cell line has no functional Rb. The cells are grown without growth factor. Which result is predicted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: S-phase genes stay off until growth factor is added, because E2F also needs the growth factor.
choices.rationale: In this pathway growth factor acts by phosphorylating Rb, and without Rb that step is not needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: S-phase genes are off in these cells, because Rb is needed to make E2F.
choices.rationale: Rb binds E2F and does not make it, so losing Rb frees E2F and does not remove it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cells arrest in G2, because Rb acts only at the G2 checkpoint.
choices.rationale: The stem places Rb's role at the control of S-phase genes in G1, and not at G2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: E2F is free and S-phase genes are expressed, so the cells can enter S phase without growth factor.
choices.rationale: Correct: Rb normally holds E2F inactive; without Rb, E2F is released regardless of growth factor, so S-phase genes can be turned on and cells can pass the G1 checkpoint.

title: link loss of a checkpoint protein to cell-cycle behavior using data (variant 2)
stem: Normal fibroblasts (N) and tumor cells (T) are grown in culture. At low density they divide at the same rate. At high density, 95% of N cells are in G1 or G0 and stop dividing, but 30% of the T cells are still in S phase and the cells pile into layers. Adding 10 times more growth factor does not restart the N cells at high density. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: T cells divide faster than N cells at all densities.
choices.rationale: The stem states that the rates are the same at low density.

choices.label: B
choices.text: N cells stop at high density because they ran out of growth factor.
choices.rationale: Adding 10 times more growth factor did not restart the N cells, so lack of growth factor is not the cause.

choices.label: C
choices.text: T cells at high density are in G0, which lets them pile up.
choices.rationale: 30% of the T cells are in S phase, so they are cycling and are not in G0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: T cells do not respond to the signals that normally stop the cycle at high density, while N cells do.
choices.rationale: Correct: the two lines act the same at low density but differ at high density, so T cells have lost response to the stop signals; the extra growth factor shows N cells did not stop for lack of it.

title: link loss of a checkpoint protein to cell-cycle behavior using data (variant 3)
stem: A drug that prevents spindle formation is added to cells. In normal cells, 85% stop with condensed chromosomes and no anaphase. In cells that lack Mad2, a spindle checkpoint protein, most cells leave mitosis within 1.5 hours with unaligned chromosomes and produce daughter cells with abnormal chromosome numbers. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mad2 is needed to condense chromosomes, because the cells lacking it have abnormal chromosome numbers.
choices.rationale: Chromosomes condense in both groups, and the problem is how they are divided.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The spindle checkpoint normally delays anaphase until the chromosomes are attached to the spindle, so cells without Mad2 divide with misaligned chromosomes.
choices.rationale: Correct: normal cells wait before anaphase when the spindle is missing; cells lacking Mad2 do not wait and divide anyway, producing cells with the wrong number of chromosomes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mad2 is needed to build the spindle, because the drug blocks spindle formation in the cells lacking Mad2.
choices.rationale: The drug prevents spindle formation in both groups, so the missing spindle comes from the drug and not from the loss of Mad2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mad2 drives cells through anaphase, because cells without Mad2 leave mitosis more slowly.
choices.rationale: Cells lacking Mad2 leave mitosis sooner, within 1.5 hours, and not more slowly.
